relearning.title: Read: the structure of DNA
relearning.description: A short reading with the twisted-ladder analogy, worked examples and quick checks.

body.text:
**I can describe the structure of DNA and the double helix model.**

**Think of a ladder that has been twisted like a spiral staircase.** A ladder has two side rails and rungs that connect them. DNA has the same parts. That twisted shape is called a **double helix** ("double" because there are two strands, "helix" because it spirals).

**The building block is a nucleotide.** Each nucleotide has three parts: a **phosphate**, a sugar called **deoxyribose**, and a **nitrogen base**. There are four bases: **adenine (A)**, **thymine (T)**, **cytosine (C)** and **guanine (G)**.

**The sides of the ladder** are made of sugar and phosphate, alternating: sugar, phosphate, sugar, phosphate. This is called the **sugar-phosphate backbone**.

**The rungs of the ladder** are pairs of bases, one from each strand, held together by weak **hydrogen bonds**. The bases always pair the same way. This is the **base pairing rule**: **A pairs with T**, and **C pairs with G**.

**Worked example:** One strand of DNA reads ATTGCA. Pair each base: A→T, T→A, T→A, G→C, C→G, A→T. The other strand reads **TAACGT**.

checks.prompt: Which three parts make up one DNA nucleotide?

options.text: A phosphate, a ribose sugar and an amino acid
A phosphate, a deoxyribose sugar and a nitrogen base
A nitrogen base, a hydrogen bond and a protein

checks.explanation: A DNA nucleotide is a phosphate, the sugar deoxyribose and one nitrogen base (A, T, C or G). Ribose is the sugar in RNA, and amino acids build proteins, not DNA.

checks.prompt: One DNA strand reads GCTA. Type the bases on the matching strand.
checks.explanation: G pairs with C, C with G, T with A and A with T, so GCTA pairs with CGAT. Pairing A with G, or writing U (an RNA base), is the common mistake.

sections.title: Chargaff's rule and who found the helix

body.text:
**Who figured it out?** In 1952, **Rosalind Franklin** made an X-ray picture of DNA (Photo 51) that showed an X pattern, a sign of a helix. In 1953, **James Watson and Francis Crick** used her picture and other data to build the double helix model.

**Chargaff's rule.** Because A always pairs with T, a DNA molecule has the **same amount of A as T**. Because C always pairs with G, it has the **same amount of C as G**. All four percentages add up to 100%.

**Worked example 2:** A DNA sample is 30% adenine. T = A, so T = 30%. A + T = 60%, which leaves 100 − 60 = 40% for C and G. Split it evenly: **C = 20% and G = 20%**.

**Worked example 3:** A sample is 15% cytosine. G = C = 15%. C + G = 30%, which leaves 70% for A and T, so **A = 35% and T = 35%**.

**Why the rungs are always the same width.** A and G are big bases, and T and C are small bases. Each rung is one big base plus one small base, so every rung is the same length and the ladder stays even.

**The two strands run in opposite directions.** One strand runs "up" and the other runs "down", like the two lanes of a highway. This is called **antiparallel**.

**Watch out for:** putting U (uracil) in DNA (U is only in RNA), pairing A with G or C with T, saying the bases form the sides (the sides are sugar and phosphate), and forgetting to split the leftover percentage in half.

checks.prompt: A DNA sample is 40% guanine. What percentage is adenine?
checks.explanation: G = C = 40%, so C + G = 80%. That leaves 20% for A and T, and half of it is A: 10%. Picking 20% forgets to split the leftover between A and T.

checks.prompt: Which part of DNA forms the rungs of the ladder?
checks.explanation: The rungs are base pairs (A–T and C–G) held by hydrogen bonds. Sugar and phosphate make the sides, which is the part students often mix up.

sections.shortAnswer: Explain how the base pairing rule lets you figure out one strand of DNA if you know the other.

cards.back: The building block of DNA: a phosphate, a deoxyribose sugar and a nitrogen base.
The sugar in DNA. It alternates with phosphate to make the sides of the ladder.
A pairs with T, and C pairs with G. They form the rungs of the ladder.
The weak bonds that hold the two bases of each rung together, so the strands can unzip.

checks.prompt: Which base pairs with cytosine (C) in DNA?
checks.explanation: C always pairs with G, and A always pairs with T. Pairing C with T is the common mix-up.

checks.prompt: What makes up the sides (the backbone) of the DNA ladder?
checks.explanation: The sides are sugar, phosphate, sugar, phosphate. The bases are the rungs, and hydrogen bonds hold the rungs together.

checks.prompt: One DNA strand reads TTAG. Type the bases on the matching strand.
checks.explanation: T→A, T→A, A→T, G→C, so TTAG pairs with AATC. Writing U instead of T is the common mistake: U is only in RNA.

body.problem: A DNA sample is 22% adenine (A). Find the percentage of thymine (T), cytosine (C) and guanine (G).

steps.text: A always pairs with T, so there is the same amount of each. T = 22%.
Add A and T: 22% + 22% = 44%. All four bases add up to 100%, so C and G share what is left: 100% − 44% = 56%.
C always pairs with G, so they are equal. Split 56% in half: C = 28% and G = 28%.
Check your work: 22 + 22 + 28 + 28 = 100. The answer is T = 22%, C = 28%, G = 28%.

checks.prompt: Your turn: a sample is 35% thymine. What percent is adenine? Type a number.
checks.explanation: A pairs with T, so A = T = 35%. Subtracting from 100 (65) is the common mistake. That is the amount left for C and G together.

checks.prompt: A sample is 18% cytosine. What percent is adenine?
checks.explanation: G = C = 18%, so C + G = 36%. That leaves 64% for A and T, and half is A: 32%. Picking 64% forgets to split the leftover in half.

checks.prompt: In the twisted-ladder model of DNA, what holds the two bases of each rung together?
checks.explanation: Weak hydrogen bonds hold each base pair together. Sugar and phosphate make the sides of the ladder, not the rungs.

checks.prompt: One DNA strand reads CATG. Type the bases on the matching strand.
checks.explanation: Use the base pairing rule: C→G, A→T, T→A, G→C, so the matching strand is GTAC. Pairing A with G or C with T is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: A DNA sample is 10% cytosine. What percentage is thymine?
checks.explanation: G = C = 10%, so C + G = 20%. That leaves 80% for A and T, split evenly: T = 40%. Forgetting to split the leftover in half (80%) is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Which base is found in RNA but never in DNA?
checks.explanation: DNA's four bases are A, T, C and G. Uracil (U) is only in RNA, so it never belongs in a DNA strand.
